info.title: Integrating Siliko Core into Your Program

article.para: Siliko Core provides an interface to integrate parsing and mathematical evaluation into a program. A developer can use the simple infix parser with the built-in set of functions to provide basic functionality, or write their own parser for another syntax, or add additional, custom functions to the lnguage.

section.para: Siliko Core includes 13 public header files:

listitem.para:
Master header, includes all other headers

section.para: Each header file is associated with a component of Siliko Core, such as in-language functions, the lexer, parser, and so on. For an exact listing of which types and functions are in each header, see the API Reference.

The SilikoCore/Value.h header contains three types. The SilikoValue type represents a value passed to and yielded by the Siliko Core library. The SilikoValueStatus enumeration represents which type of value a SilikoValue holds: an integer (SilikoValueInteger), a real number (SilikoValueReal), or an error (SilikoValueError). The SilikoError enumeration represents an error that Siliko Core can encounter while parsing or evaluating expressions, for example a syntax error (SilikoErrorSyntax) or a division by zero error (SilikoErrorZeroDivision). For a full list of error values, see The SilikoError entry in the API Reference.
To make a SilikoValue object, you can use the functions, SilikoValueCreateFromInteger, or SilikoValueCreateFromReal. These functions take a long long int, and double, respectively.

para.programlisting: SilikoValue forty_two = SilikoValueCreateFromInteger(42); SilikoValue pi = SilikoValueCreateFromReal(3.14);

section.para: You can use the SilikoValueGetStatus function to determine what type of value a SilikoValue holds. Then, based on which type it has, you can use one of SilikoValueGetError, SilikoValueGetInteger, or SilikoValueGetReal to retrieve the value.
In the tutorial program, the SilikoValue object returned by the parser was simply printed. In a more complex scenario, one might imagine using programming logic based on the value of a SilikoValue.
And finally, as we see in this example, when you are done with a SilikoValue you must call SilikoFunctionDestroy on the SilikoValue to avoid memory leaks.

To provide input to a parser, you must build a SilikoInput object that Siliko Core’s lexical analyzer (or tokenizer) can use to read input text. To keep the input as versitle as possible, Siliko Core allows you to construct your own SilikoInput behavior to allow for various and disparate sources, such as custom string types, network connections, files, or anything else that might be developed.
Siliko Core provides a StringInput implementation that takes a C string as its source.
The SilikoStringInputCreate function will copy the string passed to it, and build a new SilikoInput object that will read characters from the copied string.

A SilikoInput has five importantant pieces. First, it has a state object. This is what you use to keep track of what position you are in, which resources you are using, and so on. This should be a custom structure that you arrange however you need to fit your custom input. The other parts are three function that act on the state object, and a SilikoInputVTable structure that that has pointers to those three functions.

The advance pointer points to a function that is used to advance the input stream by one character. The getCharacter pointer points to a function that returns the current character from the input stream, and the destroy pointer points to a function that cleans up and deletes the state object when the input is no longer needed.

Siliko Core’s lexer expects data sources to provide a sequence of characters. Since it occasionally needs to read the current character multiple times, it uses separate `Advance` and `Get` functions to move forward in the sequence, and read the current character respectively.

The `Advance` function should move to the next character in the input source, if possible, and return a true value (internally Siliko Core uses `-1`), if there are more characters to read, and return a false value (`0`) if the input has been exhausted.

The `Get` function returns the current character in the sequence. Once the `Advance` function returns false, indicating the end of input, the `Get` function’s return value should be the null character, `\0`.

The `Delete` function must free up any resources used by the `State` object including deallocating the `State` object itself. So, if the `State` object was allocated with `malloc`, the `State` object should be passed to the `free` function.

Siliko Core’s built-in lexer reads characters from a data source, groups them into *lexemes* and produces a series of *tokens* from those lexemes. A *lexeme* is a sequence of one or more characters that the lexer recognises as having some meaning, such as the single characters `+` and `/` used to represent addition and division operations, and multicharacter lexemes such as integer values like `42` and floating point values like `125.0625`, and names like `abs` and `floor`. A *token* is a representation of what that lexeme represents. For example, if the lexeme `42` is input, that would produce a token such as “Integer with value 42”.

The lexer recognizes the following as single-character lexemes: `+`, `-`, `/`, `*`, `^`, `,`, `(`, `)`. When the lexer encounters any one of these characters, it stops processing and yeilds a single-character token matching the lexeme. The build-in lexer also recognizes d as a single-character operator, but will look at the next character to make sure it’s not part of a name before yielding a token.

The tokenizer will recognize the lexemes `e` and `pi` as floating-point values, and yield floating-point tokens representing their values. The parser using the built-in lexer will not see any difference between these lexemes, and their same values entered manually. That is, `e` will yield a token of “floating-point value: 2.71828183” and `pi` will yield a token of “floating-point value: 3.14159265”.

Beyond these, the tokenizer recognizes a sequence of chatacters, starting with a letter as an ID, a sequence of numeric digits without a decimal point as an integer, and a sequence of numeric digits, including a single decimal point, as a floating-point number.
The first step to using Siliko Core’s lexer is to set one up with the `SilikoLexerNew` function. It takes a pointer to a previously constructed `SilikoDataSource` object as its sole argument.
After that point, you can use the `SilikoLexerGetToken` to get the next token. The Lexer will hold on to this token until `SilikoLexerNext` is called to advance to the next token.
If you write a parser using `SilikoLexer`, you can build it using any techniques requiring one token of look ahead.

Siliko Core uses its own hash table to look up functions such as `sin` and `abs`. This function lookup mechanism is also how arithmetic operations such as addition (`+`) and exponentiation (`^`) are handled. Because of this, before Siliko can evaluate anything, a program must first initialize a lookup table. Siliko uses the `SilikoFunctionCaller` type for this. To create a new `SilikoFunctionCaller` object, use the `SilikoFunctionCallerNew` function.

A new function caller has no functions in its lookup table. Siliko Core provides two built-in sets of functions, one set implements the basic operators used by the built-in infix parser, and the other is a set of typical math functions included in C’s `math.h` header.

Both of these functions take a pointer to a `SilikoFunctionCaller` object, and return an `int` indicating whether it was able to install all of the functions it’s supposed to install or not. A false value indicates that a memory error occured. When this happens, the list of available functions in the function caller is unspecified.

Siliko implements syntax trees with a single type, `SilikoSyntaxTreeNode`. A node can hold one of two kinds of data, a branch, or a leaf. A leaf has a single `SilikoValue` object, and a branch has a function call, and an array of child `SilikoSyntaxTreeNode` objects representing the arguments to the operation or function the branch represents. Each node can be evaluated, to yield a `SiikoValue` object with the results.
There are five functions that will create a syntax tree node:

listitem.para: SilikoSyntaxTreeNewInteger generates a leaf node with an integer value.
SilikoSyntaxTreeNewFloat generates a leaf node with a floating-point value.
SilikoSyntaxTreeNewError generates a leaf node representing a syntax error.
SilikoSyntaxTreeNewBranch generates a branch node, taking the function name as its argument.

SilikoSyntaxTreeNewNothing generates a null node. This is used to represent when a parser component reports that is has no more to process or that it didn’t receive any tokens representing the rule that it handles.

section.para: Each of these functions returns a pointer to a `SilikoSyntaxTree` that will subsequently need to be passed to `SilikoSyntaxTreeDelete` to release resources. If you pass a branch node to `SilikoSyntaxTreeDelete`, it will also call itself on any nodes in the branch’s array of child nodes.
To combine syntax tree nodes into a tree, you will need to use the *Push* functions with a branch node and another node to be added as a child node to the branch node.
For example, let’s say you wish to construct a syntax tree representing the expression `2 + 3`. You would first construct a branch node, and two leaf nodes to represent the operands.

You can create nodes in any order, so it doesn’t mater if you start with the leaves or the branch. There are two functions that add new children to a branch node, `SilikoSyntaxTreePushLeft`, and `SilikoSyntaxTreePushRight`. `SilikoSyntaxTreePushLeft` will add the new child node to the left side of the operands list, while `SilikoSyntaxTreePushRight` adds the new child to the right side. Once a syntax tree is fully assembled, it can be evaluated with the `SilikoSyntaxTreeEvaluate` function. The function takes two arguments: a `SilikoSyntaxTreeNode` pointer, and a `SilikoFunctionCaller` pointer. The syntax tree should have no remaining `NULL` nodes, and the function caller will need to have any functions referenced by the syntax tree. If syntax tree contains any `NULL` nodes, it will evaluate to a `SILIKO_VAL_SYNTAX_ERR` indicating a syntax error, and if the function caller fails to find a function name used, it will yield a `SILIKO_VAL_BAD_FUNCTION` status indicating that it failed to find a function.
If you used the above example, `Result` should have a `Status` of `SILIKO_VAL_INTEGER` and `Result.Integer` would have a value of `56` which is the result of `2 * 3 + 10 * (35 / 7)`.

To put it all together, Siliko includes an infix parser. It exposes a single function, `SilikoParseInfix`. It takes a pointer to a `SilikoDataSource` object, and returns a pointer to a `SilikoSyntaxTreeNode` object representing the root node of the syntax tree parsed out by the infix parser.
Like any other `SilikoSyntaxTreeNode`, you may call `SilikoSyntaxTreeEvaluate` to evaluate the tree and get the resulting value.
